Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Nun
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Vignette:
Sister Carmen Reyes was forty-four years old, a nun, and she had not always been one. Before taking her vows, she had been married, had built a life that ended in divorce, and then, in her late thirties, she had found her way to the cloister. Now she lived in a small religious community in a city that had once felt safe. That changed on a Tuesday afternoon in October, when she was helping to distribute food at a downtown parish outreach center. A man walked in with a backpack, and then there was noise—not a bang so much as a tearing of the world. The lights went out. When they came back, blood was everywhere: on the floor, on her white habit, on the face of a woman who had been standing next to her and was no longer standing. Sister Carmen herself had been knocked to the ground. A piece of metal had lodged in her thigh. The physical pain, sharp and hot, was the first thing she remembered clearly. The rest came later, in fragments she could not control.

In the months after the attack, Sister Carmen’s life grew small. She could no longer attend Mass in the main chapel because it was too crowded, too open, too full of people whose movements felt unpredictable. Her superior allowed her to pray alone in a small side room, but even there she found herself scanning the walls for exits, noting the placement of the fire extinguisher, the window that might serve as a way out. She had come to believe that danger was always near, that only a very limited number of spaces were truly safe: her own cell, the infirmary, the enclosed garden at night when no one else was there. The rest of the world felt like a trap.

She avoided intimacy most of all. When her fellow sisters reached out to comfort her—a hand on her shoulder, a shared prayer in the evening—she pulled back. Emotional closeness terrified her because it meant lowering her guard, and to lower her guard was to invite the memory in. And the memory came whether she wanted it or not. Sometimes she woke from a nightmare drenched in sweat, the dream’s residue clinging to her like smoke: the smell of dust and cordite, the sound of screaming, the sensation of that sharp pain in her thigh. At those moments it was not a memory at all; it was happening again, completely real across all her senses. Yet if someone asked her to describe the event deliberately, she found she could not. The details scattered like startled birds. She could access only the fragments, never the whole. She would go over and over them in her mind, trying to piece together a sequence that made sense, trying to understand why she had survived and others had not. The guilt was a constant companion.

Her work suffered. As a nun, she had once visited the sick and the elderly, but she could no longer bring herself to walk through the hospital corridors. There were crowds there, and blood—the sight of a single drop on a bandage made her stomach clench and her heart race. She stopped leaving the convent except for absolute necessities. When she did go out, she always identified escape routes before she felt comfortable anywhere. She planned how she would run, where she would hide, what she would do if the world tore open again.

What finally brought her to seek help was not her own distress—she had learned to endure that—but the concern of her Mother Superior, who had found her one morning sitting on the floor of the garden, unable to move or speak, her hand pressed to her thigh where the scar still ached. Sister Carmen had been trying to deliberately recall the moment of the explosion, trying to force it into order, and instead she had lost herself entirely. She agreed to see a therapist because she was afraid of what would happen if she did not: that the walls of her safe zone would keep shrinking until there was no room left for anyone, not even God. She hoped, though she barely dared to say it, that someone could help her find a way back to a life that was not composed entirely of escape routes.
